videos.title: How Smiling Can Increase Endurance | Ross Edgley
videos.description:
My guest on the Huberman lab podcast this week is Ross Edgley — a British ultra-endurance athlete and author known for completing extraordinary athletic feats by tapping into diverse sources of motivation and resilience.

We discuss the psychological and biological forces that allow people to persevere through extreme challenges.

Then we cover how to dynamically update your sense of purpose, emotions, philosophy, and personal narratives to expand your ability to overcome adversity of all kinds. We also discuss the brain circuits and science of fatigue and stress adaptation.

Ultimately, a new framework emerges that you can use to access persistent motivation.

This episode discusses neural circuits and biology related to motivation not previously covered on the Huberman Lab podcast.

And if you have topics or guest, you’d like me to consider for future episodes of the podcast, please put that in the comments below.

And as always, thank you for your interest in science!

videos.title: I tested 4 AI agents on 9 real tasks. Here’s who won.
videos.description:
I have personal-agent fatigue, so I ran the first How I AI personal-agent benchmark: Grok Bot, Dot, Muse, and Claude Duet across nine real tasks, from a Slack reply and a Sentry bug to a Figma thumbnail, inbox triage, a family newspaper, physics homework for a fourth grader, shoe shopping, and a ChatPRD launch video. I used computer use to operate them: Claude ran Dot, Codex ran the rest and scored the results live. Here’s the scoreboard—and which agent I’d actually trust for work vs. life.

videos.title: There Are 3 Types of Failure. Only 1 Is Good.
videos.description:
Purpose: Go to https://solved.deals/purpose to start getting unstuck today.
Waking Up: Get started at https://manson.deals/wakingup for a 14 day trial, no risk.

Forgetting to hit send and launching a business that flops both count as failure, but they shouldn't get the same reaction. Drew and I wrap up this episode through a story of a young Harvard researcher who found that the best hospital teams reported the most mistakes. She thought she'd botched her research, until she realized what was really going on. Her work gives us three types of failure: the kind to fix and forget, the kind to catch early, and the kind worth chasing for the lesson. We also share why a failed startup barely improves your odds the second time, five questions that tell you whether it's time to quit, and why the right moment to quit almost always feels too early.
